title: Ten Shapes, and Two That Lie

lessons.title: ০ (digit zero) — the Bengali zero
lessons.gloss: the Bengali zero — the same ring, in the same place, meaning the same thing

notice.text: Before we start: this one needs your hands, so it is not a driving lesson. You will want a pen and something to write on and your eyes, for letter shapes on the page. segments.text: Sixty script lessons have taught you letters. Reading কালো is reading letters. Every one of the twelve lessons ahead of you puts something on the page that is not a letter at all, and this book has never done that before.
০ (digit zero).
That is the Bengali digit zero.
Put it beside the zero you already read: 0. A ring, closed, standing on the line, meaning none. Bengali writes it the same way, and means the same thing.

That is not a coincidence and it is worth knowing before the other nine arrive. Wikipedia describes the Bengali numerals as a variety of the Hindu–Arabic numeral system — the same system as the digits on your keyboard, not a rival one. They are positional, they are read left to right, and ০ (digit zero) does the same job at the end of a number as 0 does at the end of 10.
There is no Bengali WORD for zero in this book yet. Today it is a shape you can read.

segments.instruction: ০ (digit zero)
the five numbers you can already count — ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch
segments.source: [YOU SAY: the five numbers you can already count — *ek, dui, tin, chār, pā̃ch*]

feedback.incorrect: Compare it with the 0 you already read.

segments.text: What is ০ (digit zero)? (Zero.) Is it a letter? (No — the first thing in this book that is not.) Which system do the Bengali digits belong to? (The same one as 0–9.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart; Wikipedia: Bengali–Assamese numerals.

segments.text: ২ (digit two).
That is the Bengali digit two, and you can say it: দুই.

Set it beside 2. The top curls the other way and the foot is a diagonal rather than a bar, but the gross shape is the same — a turn at the top, a stroke running down to the right. Nobody would call ২ (digit two) a two from nothing; anybody who already reads 2 can be told once and keep it.

So the count of shapes that cost you almost nothing now stands at two, and both of them mean exactly what the shape you already know means. Remember that. It stops being true in this chapter, and the place where it stops is the whole point of the chapter.

segments.text: What is ২ (digit two)? (Two — দুই.) What is ২০? (Twenty.) How many shapes so far have meant the same as the shape you already knew? (Both of them.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: ী hangs on a letter and cannot stand alone. A digit is the opposite: it stands alone and hangs on nothing. Keep that difference in front of you, because this one looks like a letter.
৩ (digit three).
That is the Bengali digit three, and you can say it: তিন.
Now put it beside a letter you have had since the opening chapters:
They are the same rounded body. ও carries a stroke down its right-hand side; ৩ (digit three) does not, and that is the entire difference between a number and a letter here.
This is the only digit in the chapter that collides with a Bengali letter you have been taught, and the fix is one stroke wide: if it has the tail on the right, it is a letter.

segments.text: ১ (digit one).
That is the Bengali digit one, and you can say it: এক.

Nothing helps you here. 1 is a bare stroke; ১ (digit one) is a curl that starts high, comes down and hooks back to the right at the foot. There is no shape you already own to hang it on, and no letter it can be confused with.
That is worth naming rather than hiding: ০ (digit zero), ২ (digit two) and ৩ (digit three) each arrived carrying something. This one is simply learned, and so are the two after it.
Read ১০ — one, then zero. Ten.

segments.instruction: ১ (digit one)

acceptedResponses: one zero three — a hundred and three

feedback.correct: Three digits, read left to right, exactly as you would read 103.
feedback.incorrect: Take the digits one at a time from the left.

segments.text: What is ১ (digit one)? (One — এক.) What did it bring with it that the first three digits did? (Nothing.) What is ১০? (Ten.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.instruction: read তিন off the page — R4, eighty lessons back

segments.text: That last recall is the one this chapter exists for. তিন is the word three, spelled with three letters, and you have been able to read it for eighty lessons. ৩ (digit three) is the digit 3, and until two lessons ago you could not read it at all. A book can print either one, and they are not the same object.
৫ (digit five).
That is the Bengali digit five, and you can say it: পাঁচ.
Another one that brings nothing: a hooked stroke over an open bowl, like a C with a lid. 5 will not help you and no Bengali letter you know is close to it.
You can now read every number written out of ০ (digit zero) ১ (digit one) ২ (digit two) ৩ (digit three) ৫ (digit five), which is most of a page number and all of a small count.

feedback.correct: Read left to right, like any number.
feedback.incorrect: One digit at a time, starting on the left.

segments.text: What is ৫ (digit five)? (Five — পাঁচ.) What is the difference between তিন and ৩ (digit three)? (One is the word, the other is the digit.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: ৬ (digit six).

That is the Bengali digit six: a bowl at the foot with a tail rising away to the right. 6 does not help — its loop is at the bottom left and its stem comes down from above, which is nearly the reverse.

And here your count runs out. This book has taught you এক to পাঁচ and no further, so you can now read a number you have no Bengali word for. That is a real gap and it is worth stating plainly rather than covering: from here to the end of the chapter you are learning to READ four numbers you cannot yet SAY. The words are a separate piece of work.
Reading is still worth having on its own. A page number, a price and a date are all read far more often than they are said aloud.

segments.text: কাপড় is the first thing this book taught you that has a price on it. Hold on to it; you will read a price before this chapter ends.
৮ (digit eight).
That is the Bengali digit eight: an upright stroke with a single small bowl at the bottom right — much closer to a lower-case b than to anything numeric.

Look hard at it and notice what it is not. It has one bowl. 8 has two, stacked. Whatever the two-loop shape means in Bengali, it does not mean eight — and something has to mean it, because the shape exists.
That is the next lesson, and it is the one place in this chapter where the digits you already read will tell you a lie.

segments.text: What is ৮ (digit eight)? (Eight.) How many bowls does it have? (One.) What does the two-bowl shape mean in Bengali? (Not eight — and you are about to find out what.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: ৪ (digit four).
That is the Bengali digit four, and you can say it: চার.
It is two loops, stacked. It is the shape of an 8.

headers: in the digits you already read
utterances: shape: two stacked loops. in the digits you already read: eight. in Bengali: four.
shape: upright with one bowl. in the digits you already read: nothing. in Bengali: eight.

segments.text: Read the top row again. Every reflex you have says eight, and it is wrong by four every single time — on a price, on a bus number, on a year.

The first three digits of this chapter arrived meaning exactly what their shape already meant to you. This one arrives meaning something else, and it is not a near miss: ৪ (digit four) and 8 are the same drawing.
The defence is the lesson before this one. If you are unsure, ask how many bowls: two bowls is four; one bowl is eight.

segments.instruction: ৪ (digit four)
চার, then read ৪ (digit four), ৪৮, ৮৪

segments.prompt: Read these two in order, and do not trust your eye: ৪ (digit four) ৮ (digit eight)

feedback.correct: Two bowls first, one bowl second.
feedback.incorrect: Count the bowls. Two is four; one is eight.
The first shape is four, however much it looks like an eight.

segments.text: What is ৪ (digit four)? (Four — চার.) What does your eye want it to be? (Eight.) Which question settles it? (How many bowls?)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart; Wiktionary: ৪ (digit four).

segments.text: ৯ (digit nine).
That is the Bengali digit nine: a small closed body with a tail sweeping up and away to the right.
Once again, look at what it is not. 9 is a ring with a straight stem dropping below it. ৯ (digit nine) has no dropped stem at all; its tail goes the other way, upward.

You have seen this pattern one lesson ago. The Bengali digit for eight did not take the 8 shape, and the 8 shape turned out to belong to four. The Bengali digit for nine does not take the 9 shape either — so ask the same question. Something takes it.

feedback.incorrect: Neither of them is what its shape suggests in the digits you grew up with.

segments.text: What is ৯ (digit nine)? (Nine.) Does it look like 9? (No — the tail goes up, not down.) Which two Bengali digits have now refused the shape you expected? (Eight and nine.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: ৭ (digit seven).
That is the Bengali digit seven, and it is the shape of a 9: a closed body at the top with a straight stem dropping from its right side.
The chapter's second false friend, and the last shape in the set:

headers: in the digits you already read
utterances: shape: two stacked loops. in the digits you already read: eight. in Bengali: four.
shape: body with a dropped stem. in the digits you already read: nine. in Bengali: seven.

segments.text: Both lies run the same way. In each case the Bengali digit for that value — ৮ (digit eight) for eight, ৯ (digit nine) for nine — took a different shape, leaving the familiar one standing empty; and in each case a smaller number moved into it.

Two out of ten shapes will actively mislead you. The other eight will not. That ratio is worth carrying, because it is the reason to slow down on exactly two shapes rather than to distrust the whole page.

segments.text: Ten shapes are in your hand. Here they are in order:
০ (digit zero) ১ (digit one) ২ (digit two) ৩ (digit three) ৪ (digit four) ৫ (digit five) ৬ (digit six) ৭ (digit seven) ৮ (digit eight) ৯ (digit nine) (the ten digits).
A rule with an edge at each end, and both edges matter:

utterances: the band: where the shapes AGREE. what it means for you: ০ (digit zero) is a 0 and means zero. ২ (digit two) is close to a 2 and means two. Trust these.

the band: where they are simply NEW. what it means for you: ১ (digit one) ৩ (digit three) ৫ (digit five) ৬ (digit six) ৮ (digit eight) ৯ (digit nine) carry no Western digit's shape at all, so there is nothing to be misled by. ৩ (digit three) is the one to watch against a letter, not against a digit: ও is the same body with a stroke down its right side.
the band: where they LIE. what it means for you: ৪ (digit four) is drawn as an 8 and means four. ৭ (digit seven) is drawn as a 9 and means seven. Nowhere else.

segments.text: Two of ten. Say them as a pair and they stay a pair: the eight is a four, the nine is a seven — and in both cases the Bengali digit that really means eight or nine is a shape you would never mistake for anything.
That is the whole rule. Eight shapes ask you to learn them; two ask you to un-learn something first.

segments.text: Which two shapes mislead? (The 8-shape, which is four; the 9-shape, which is seven.) Which digit is confusable with a letter rather than with a digit? (৩ (digit three), against ও.) How many of the ten are safe? (Eight.)
Sources: Unicode Bengali chart.

segments.text: Sixty script lessons taught you letters, and one of them, long ago, taught you to read তিন. That was the word. Until this chapter you could not read ৩ (digit three), and so you could not read a price, a date, a clock face or a page number — the things a reader meets far more often than they meet a sentence.

Ten shapes closed that. Eight of them were simply learned; ০ (digit zero) and ২ (digit two) cost almost nothing because the Bengali digits and the digits on your keyboard are one system rather than two; and two of them — ৪ (digit four) and ৭ (digit seven) — had to be taken away from a reflex before they could be given to you.

What this chapter did not do is teach you to SAY six, seven, eight, nine or zero. Those words are not in this book yet. You can read every number on the page and speak the first five of them, and the gap between those two abilities is now the most useful thing left undone in this column.
Read ৪৭. (Forty-seven — not ninety-eight.) Which numbers can you now read? (All of them.) Which can you say? (One to five.)
